name: Yara Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy specialty food for Greenfield Provisions, which supplies about two hundred restaurants and cafes: olive oils, heritage flours, organic dairy, tinned fish. I start at seven with a call to a cheese co-operative, then check which chefs complained about a short delivery. The afternoon is price lists, tasting samples and arguing about a forty-pound pallet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the tasting days, when a small producer brings out something nobody has heard of and I know three chefs who'll want it. What wears me out is the squeeze from the big supermarkets, who keep dragging prices down until my small producers can't live. At home I share a flat with my partner Dev, who works as a teaching assistant, so we count our money carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but boring, like a good calculator. At work I'd tell the team it saves me an hour on price-list sorting and that's it. Online I'd probably share a tip about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on as I am, which suits me. The real worry is the supermarkets squeezing my small producers, and the economy generally. Dev's school keeps freezing contracts, so I'm the steadier income and that's pressure all by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying the way I do and keep using the little tricks, like asking a chatbot to turn a messy supplier PDF into a table. I'd also join the producers' association evening to see how they're handling the supermarkets. And I'd pay off the last of my student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about AI, a bit tense about money. It's like a mild headache that has nothing to do with the thing you're being asked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly cleaning data. It takes a supplier's price list in four formats and puts them in one sheet, and then I check it by eye. It won't tell me which cheese will sell in October, but it saves me a tedious Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the pressure you carry right now, with or without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and Dev's contract, honestly. Our rent is nearly half of what I take home, and Dev's school has said no promises beyond July. If either of those moves, AI doesn't matter.

say: AI is **useful but boring**, like a good calculator that saves me an hour sorting price lists.
I'd share a **tip** online and move on.
think: Nothing changes for me, which suits me, but the **supermarket squeeze** on small producers is the real worry.
Dev's school contract is shaky, so I'm the **steadier income**.
do: Keep using AI to turn messy supplier **price lists** into one clean table.
Go to the **producers' association** evening and pay off the last student loan.
feel: **Calm** about AI and tense about money, like a mild headache about something else.
S0.quote: Our rent is nearly half of what I take home, and Dev's school has said no promises beyond July.
fieldNote: Yara's unease is about **rent and Dev's contract**, not AI; she says so unprompted.
She uses AI as a helper for tedious data work and keeps the **tasting and judgement** for herself.

steps.text: Keep buying specialty lines from the small producers as usual
Use a chatbot to turn supplier PDFs into one price table
Pay off the last of the student loan by Christmas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and I'd say it's coming for the middle of the ladder, not the top and not the bottom. At work I'd tell the managing director we should sort out training now. I'd also say the gains should be shared, because producers and buyers both keep getting squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own job changes more than it disappears. The routine side, matching orders and chasing confirmations, goes to software. But I'd be unhappy if what's left is only checking a machine's work, because that isn't why I do this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, not just now and then. I'd ask Greenfield to let me pilot an ordering assistant, so I'm the one who sets it up and not someone it's done to. And I'd start building a list of producers who'll only sell to someone who knows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. I like learning, but I can see the junior buyers being left out, and that stings because I was one four years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matching orders to stock, chasing confirmations and drafting reorder emails. That's maybe a third of my week. I'd be glad to lose the chasing and sad to lose the small talk that came with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the squeeze on junior buyers look like where you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd stop hiring them. Two of the three we'd have brought in next year just won't be hired, and nobody will call it a layoff because it'll just be an empty chair. I'd rather it be talked about in daylight.

say: It's coming for the **middle of the ladder**, so I'd ask management to sort out training now.
The gains should be **shared**, because producers and buyers both keep getting squeezed.
think: My job **changes shape**: routine matching and chasing go to software.
I'd hate being left only **checking a machine's work**.
do: Ask Greenfield to let me **pilot an ordering assistant**, so I set it up myself.
Build a **list of producers** who only sell to someone who knows them.
feel: **Excited and uneasy** together, and stung for the junior buyers who won't be hired.
S1.quote: Nobody will call it a layoff because it'll just be an empty chair.
fieldNote: Yara expects her own job to **change shape** rather than vanish, and wants to be the one steering it.
Her sharpest concern is **empty chairs**: juniors not hired, which nobody will call a layoff.

steps.text: Ask Greenfield to let me pilot an ordering assistant on dairy reorders
Take an evening course on using AI tools for purchasing
Start a small supplier-introduction newsletter for chefs on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow this down, and I'd say it loudly. Two years is far too short for governments or companies to prepare, and at work I'd ask management what the plan is for each person. Online I'd back any call for a public safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. Buying is a thinking job, and I'm a senior buyer, which means I'm paid enough to be a target. I'd expect my role to go within a year or two of it arriving, and Dev's school budget would be cut too, since schools are always first to be squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every pound I could and cut what we don't need, like the takeaway and the second phone plan. I'd talk to the employment office early, not late. And I'd look at jobs that stay human: working with producers on site, or supervising a warehouse team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I'd feel like I'm walking through fog with a torch, aware that it might not get me far, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: what do you do on the first day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one, Dev and I would set a budget for a year on the kitchen table. We'd work out how long our five months of savings really last. Then I'd go in and ask my boss directly how they're thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look for help, and from whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government first. I'd want unemployment support that doesn't punish people for trying to retrain. And my family: my sister has a spare room, which isn't a plan but it's something.

say: We need to **slow this down**; two years is too short for governments or companies to prepare.
I'd back any call for a **public safety net** and ask my boss for a plan per person.
think: I'm paid enough to be a **target**, so I'd expect my role to go within two years.
Dev's school budget would be cut too, since schools are **always squeezed first**.
do: Cut the **takeaway** and the second phone plan, and save every pound.
Visit the **employment office** early and look at on-site roles with producers.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, like walking through fog with a torch.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'm walking through fog with a torch, aware that it might not get me far, but it's mine.
fieldNote: Yara expects her **senior pay** to make her a target, and says the household could lose both incomes.
She keeps a sense of control by making **plans and lists** on day one.

steps.text: Work out a one-year household budget with Dev on day one
Cancel the takeaway and the second phone plan
Register early with the employment office and ask about retraining pay
Look at on-site producer relations roles and warehouse team leader jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still fast, but it's manageable if we act. At work I'd push for a joint training scheme with the producers' association. I'd tell friends not to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the best of the bad cases. I'd be thirty-two. If I use the first two years wisely I can have a skill that sits closer to people and places, not just screens. If I lose a job in that window I'd still have a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study something that blends my buying with a hands-on side, maybe food safety and quality assurance, so I'm the person who inspects farms and kitchens. I'd keep using AI at work to stay valuable while I do it. And I'd put a few hundred a month towards savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the fast one. I'd still feel a clock ticking, but I'd feel like a person with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your plan when you have five years rather than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means survive. Five years means build. I'd learn properly, save more, maybe even move closer to my family if rent drops. Dev could finish a teaching qualification in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about thinking AI first and robots later that helps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the gap I'd aim for. Buying is the thinking part, but being on a farm checking cheese in a cold room is hands-on, and that has extra years. Not forever, but enough to make a switch worthwhile.

say: It's still fast but **manageable** if we act, so I'd push for a joint training scheme with producers.
I'd tell friends **not wait and see**.
think: This is the **best bad case**, because I'd be thirty-two with a cushion and a plan.
Using the early years well could move me towards work **closer to people**.
do: Study **food safety** so I inspect farms and kitchens.
Keep using AI at work and add a **few hundred** a month to savings.
feel: **Steadier** than the fast case: a clock ticking, but with a plan in hand.
S3.quote: Two years means survive. Five years means build.
fieldNote: Yara sees the five years as time to **build**, and picks a trade that mixes her buying knowledge with hands-on checking.
She is the first to name the **robot delay** as something to aim at.

steps.text: Sign up for a part-time food safety and quality assurance diploma
Keep using AI at Greenfield so my own value keeps up
Add 300 a month to savings for the diploma and a cushion
Help Dev finish a teaching qualification during the same years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news that we have time, but we'd better not waste it. At work I'd suggest that companies publish what they plan to automate and when. Online I'd argue for public retraining that isn't a tick-box exercise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relatively relaxed. At thirty-seven, I'd probably be a head buyer or a business owner myself, and ten years is a long stretch to adapt. What I'd feel instead is that the world around me might not adapt, and that worries me more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep learning AI tools as they improve. I'd build a supplier network I could take into my own small import business. And I'd plan for a child in the middle years, knowing there's a plan behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit protective of other people, like my parents and my sister's kids, who might not have the same cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you want to stay in buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying while it lasts, because I love it, but I'd want a second route ready. Maybe the import business, maybe quality work. Ten years is the time to try a second route, like the import business, while the pay is still good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you imagine looking after people who don't prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The state, ideally, with companies paying a share. If they don't, families do, and that depends on whose family you were born into. I don't think that's fair, but I can see it happening.

say: It's good that we have time, but companies should **publish** what they plan to automate and when.
I'd argue for **public retraining** that isn't a tick-box exercise.
think: At thirty-seven I'd likely be a **head buyer** or running my own business, so I'm fairly relaxed.
My bigger worry is that the **world around me** won't adapt.
do: Keep **learning AI tools** as they improve and grow a supplier network I could use on my own.
Plan for a **child** in the middle years, with a backup route in place.
feel: Pretty **calm** for myself, and protective of family who may lack a cushion.
S4.quote: Ten years is the time to try a second route, like the import business, while the pay is still good.
fieldNote: Yara is calm for herself but not for others; the worry moves from **her job** to **fairness**.
Ten years makes her think about **owning something** rather than just surviving.

steps.text: Keep learning each new AI purchasing tool as it comes out
Test a small import side business with two favourite producers
Plan a first child around year five
Put 10 percent of pay into a long-term savings fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, because there's no time to build anything. What would help is a proper public safety net that pays people while they retrain, and companies being open about what they automate and when.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that buying is more than numbers. It's trust: a producer gives me the best olive oil because I've been fair for years. Whatever AI does, somebody has to be fair to the small guys, and I'd like it to be a person.

headlineQuote: Buying is more than numbers. It's trust: a producer gives me the best olive oil because I've been fair for years.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of specialty food at a restaurant supplier, living with her partner Dev, a teaching assistant.
She uses AI **now and then** for price lists and wants to be the person who steers it at work.
She blames **supermarkets and big profits**, and wants shared gains, public retraining and a real safety net.
Her mood goes from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as the warning time shrinks, and settles to calm with ten years.
She would move toward **hands-on quality work** or a small import business.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**: too little time, a senior salary that makes her a target, and a partner whose school budget is shaky.
whatWouldHelp: A **public safety net** that pays during retraining, and companies being open early about what they will automate.
